pl-l4d16c2-d1e115.summary: States that John commands satisfaction: 'bring forth fruits worthy of penance', so that the quality and quantity of punishment accord with the quality and quantity of the fault; the fruit of good work should not be equal for one who sinned little or not at all and one who fell gravely.
claims: Satisfaction must be proportioned to the fault.

pl-l4d16c2-d1e124.summary: Quotes Augustine on the discernment the penitent needs: let him consider the quality of the crime in place, time, perseverance, person, temptation, and the manifold execution of the vice; a fornicator must repent according to his state or office, the manner of his deed, a sacred place or a holy time; how long he persisted, how hard he was tempted or whether he sought sin. All this must be confessed and lamented; he should weep for the virtue he lost, since offending in one point makes him guilty of all, and one is guiltier the more favored by God, as Adam sinned more for abounding in good.
claims: The circumstances of sin must be confessed and lamented.
One must lament the loss of virtue as well as the sin.

pl-l4d16c2-d1e139.summary: Continues Augustine: let him place himself wholly in the priest's judgment and power, ready to do for the soul's life what he would do to avoid bodily death, joyfully. Let him offer to God first his mind and contrition, then what he can of his goods, since God looked first to Abel, then his gifts. He should not, out of shame, divide his confession among priests, which is self-praise and hypocrisy; he should not approach the Lord's body before good conscience strengthens him; and he should keep from games and worldly spectacles. These are worthy fruits of penance.
claims: The penitent submits wholly to the priest's judgment.
The penitent should refrain from communion until his conscience is restored.

pl-l4d16c2-d1e152.summary: Adds Augustine: let the soul seek fruits worthy of penance, not merely worthy fruits; there are worthy fruits of virtue that do not suffice for penitents, since penance demands heavier ones, so that the dead may obtain life by grief and groaning.
claims: Fruits of virtue do not suffice for penance; heavier ones are required.

pl-l4d16c2-d1e158.summary: Draws out what worthy fruits of penance are, by which true satisfaction is fulfilled, and that not all worthy fruits are worthy fruits of penance; this concerns penance for greater crimes, since what suffices for lesser sinners does not suffice for grave ones.

pl-l4d16c2.summary: Satisfaction is commanded by John: 'bring forth fruits worthy of penance', so that the quality and quantity of punishment match the quality and quantity of the fault. The penitent needs discernment, considering, as Augustine teaches, the quality of the crime in place, time, perseverance, person, temptation, and manner; all these circumstances must be confessed and lamented, along with the virtue lost, since one who offends in one point is guilty of all. He must place himself wholly in the priest's judgment, ready to do anything for the soul's life, offer first his heart and then his goods, not divide his confession among priests out of shame, not approach the Lord's body before his conscience is restored, and abstain from games and spectacles. Some worthy fruits of virtue are not sufficient for penance, which for graver crimes demands heavier fruits.
claims: Satisfaction must match the quality and quantity of the fault.
The circumstances of sin must be considered, confessed, and lamented.
The penitent must submit wholly to the priest's judgment.
Confession must not be divided among several priests.
Graver crimes require heavier fruits of penance.
